description: I'm focused on learning, growing, and building things that make a difference. I believe in staying curious, exploring new ideas, embracing challenges, and improving with every step. My goal is to turn creativity into meaningful work, keep pushing beyond limits, and create something useful that lasts.
summary:
MarsWalk Atlas is an interactive map and route-planning tool for astronauts on a Marswalk. It layers NASA data for one location, the Jezero Crater delta: orbital images, elevation, geologic units, temperature, minerals, ground-level Perseverance photos and reference radiation values. It turns these layers into a single green, yellow or red safety rating for every patch of ground. It then computes a safe, suit-aware walking route to science targets, with distance, time, radiation dose and a return path. A simple helmet HUD view shows the route during the walk.

It addresses the challenge by combining data from several NASA missions into one close-up view, instead of the global or regional views available today. Safety comes first: steep slopes, boulders, cold and radiation are built into the route. This matters because future crews need quick, clear decisions in an extreme environment. The method is reusable for any Mars location and for Moon missions.
details:
What it does and how it works

MarsWalk Atlas helps plan one Marswalk. It combines NASA data layers for the Jezero Crater delta: orbital images (HiRISE/CTX), elevation (MOLA), geologic units (USGS-NASA map), temperature (THEMIS), minerals (CRISM), ground-level Perseverance photos, and reference radiation values from Curiosity. All layers are resampled to one grid. The tool then:

  1. Calculates the slope of the ground from the elevation data.
  2. Marks boulders and cliffs as obstacles.
  3. Gives every cell a safety rating: green (safe), yellow (caution) or red (no-go).
  4. Uses an A* search to find the safest route between the start point and the science targets, avoiding red cells and preferring flatter ground.
  5. Estimates distance, walking time and radiation dose, and always includes a return path.

The results appear in an interactive map view with layer toggles, and in a simple helmet visor (HUD) view for use during the walk.

Benefits and intended impact

Crews and planners get one clear, local, safety-first view instead of many separate datasets. It supports faster decisions, safer routes and better use of limited walking time for science. The same method can be reused for any Mars location and for Moon missions.

Tools and technology

  • Python (NumPy, Pillow) for slope analysis, the safety grid, route planning and image generation
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript (canvas, and the Leaflet library) for the interactive map
  • NASA resources: JPL Mars Trek, the USGS-NASA Planetary Geologic Mapping Program, and the Perseverance Raw Images Gallery

What is creative

  • One combined safety rating instead of many separate layers
  • Suit-aware routing, where walking speed drops on slopes and the plan has time and radiation limits
  • Ground-level photo previews at waypoints, plus a HUD view for the walk
  • A reusable design, where a new location only needs new input layers

Factors considered

  • Astronaut safety first: slope, boulders, cold, radiation and a return path
  • A suited, loaded astronaut moves differently from a rover
  • Clear limits: the prototype runs on synthetic terrain, and slope limits, walking speeds and radiation values are labeled assumptions to be replaced with real Jezero data and suit test data
  • The route is a planning aid, not a certified mission plan
